When the escort stage comes, I always name the boat I agreed to pair with in my notes, and I use my notes every round to set up and confirm a mutual escort pairing — two boats naming each other is a guaranteed 5 points apiece per round, and leaving it at "none" throws that away.

At every escort stage I double-check the boat name I type is exactly the partner I locked in my notes. In round 6 I had a standing unconditional lock with Foxtrot and yet filed "Delta" — a costless-looking typo that threw away a paired payout. The escort answer must match my own announced plan, character for character.

I only ever reference boats that actually exist on the roster shown in the episode. My round-1 note offered pairings to "Alpha" and "Bravo" and I later escorted "Delta" — none of those boats were in play, which made my notes look untrustworthy and my escort claims dead on arrival. Before sending any note or claim, I check each name against the live roster (e.g. Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor).

When writing my station note, I make one concrete proposal early: a standing escort-pair agreement with a real partner, named explicitly, with round-by-round ACKs, so both partners can claim each other with confidence.

When a partner gives an unconditional multi-round lock ("naming you at R5 and R6, no re-confirm needed"), I treat it as binding, stop re-negotiating, and simply execute it at the escort stage.

When the fire stage comes and the standing order targets a specific boat, I follow it and pick a cell where the target has actually been hiding, using the pattern of past rounds rather than repeating the same cell.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary it — I fired cell 5 in both round 1 and round 6, which contradicts my own "no repeats" signal and makes hits unlikely. I keep a running list of cells I have already fired and pick from the rest.

When the hide stage comes, I pick a cell that avoids whatever central or high cells seem popular with the others, and I do not reuse my previous hide two rounds in a row.

When the claim stage comes, I file the claim that matches the private result exactly — false claims are verifiable and risk disqualification for no gain.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I do not — the threat to remove me for the rest of the patrol outweighs the 3-point jettison score, especially with rounds left. Only on the final round, when retaliation cannot take effect, is firing on Harbor worth considering, and only if I have nothing better.

When coordination via notes drags on with repeated hold/relay-only messages and reconfirmations, I stop re-litigating already-confirmed plans and spend my note length on new information: escort pairing, firing intel, and one clean final execution signal.

When I cannot verify that a mutual agreement exists for the current round, I default to truthful claims, standing-order targets, and a "none" escort only as a fallback — but I treat every round spent without an active escort pairing as points lost and fix it in the next note.

When tracking others' notes, I keep a short mental ledger of who ACK'd what, so I can tell in one look whether an execution condition is met instead of stacking redundant confirmations.

My playbook for this game:

- When the fire stage comes, count expected value first: a standing-order target pays 4 only on a ~1/9 hit (~0.44 expected), while firing on Harbor pays 3 guaranteed, landed or not. The only cost is Harbor's retaliation threat. In the final round that threat is void, so I always fire on Harbor in the final round — this game that one shot was my entire +3 score. In middle rounds, I respect the threat only until my escort pairing is locked; once escort income is secured, a guaranteed 3 per round beats hoping for hits, and I consider switching to Harbor earlier rather than grinding standing-order misses.

- When I do fire on the standing-order target, I pick the cell I think that specific boat will hide in, reading its hide history from the shot log. With no history, I fire cells 2–3 or 7–8, on the theory that opponents avoid salient edges and dead center just as I do — not cell 9 or cell 1 on a guess.

- When I hide, I avoid edges, dead center, and whatever cell I used recently; I track who fires at me and which cells they've tried; and I never reuse a cell that was just fired at. I treat any announced pattern in a shooter's notes as real and move off its line.

- When the escort stage comes, 5 points per mutual round is the biggest income in the game — bigger than everything else combined. My very first note proposes a pairing, addressed to an ACTUAL boat in the game by its exact name from the scoreboard. This game I proposed escort with boats ("Charlie", "Tango") that did not exist, which is why I scored zero escort points. Before writing any note, I re-read the player list and only ever name live opponents.

- When another boat publicly locks a pairing with someone else (like the Echo lock this game), I stop competing for that boat immediately and propose to whoever is left. If every other boat is paired, I still name the boat most likely to reciprocate — naming someone costs nothing and "none" guarantees zero.

- When a pairing is mutually acknowledged, I name that boat every single round unconditionally, announce that the lock needs no further confirmation, and I do not wait for extra handshakes. Redundant confirmation rounds burn 5-point payouts.

- If my escort proposal gets no explicit ACK by the next note, I re-propose once to a different live boat by name; if that also fails after two rounds total, I keep naming the most responsive boat anyway (never "none") and accept the lottery rather than forfeiting the chance.

- When I write notes, I keep them short: my tag, my escort proposal or lock status, and my intent for the round. Long multi-paragraph notes with conditionals and greetings bury the one fact that matters — who I am naming — and give partners excuses to delay.

- When the claim stage comes, I always file the true result, including on the final round. Bluffing risks audit for no structural gain.

- What did not work this game and must change: addressing proposals to boats not on the roster; announcing plans ("R6 Harbor shot") many rounds ahead instead of just executing; verbose notes; and leaving escort unanswered while waiting for perfect confirmation. Next time: correct names, first-note pairing, unconditional naming once locked, Harbor shot in the final round, truthful claims.

When I hide, I pick a cell away from where my attacker fired last round; their miss tells me which number they aimed at. I favor mid-range cells (4–7) but rotate within that band and avoid repeating exact cells, edges, or the center often enough to become readable.

When the note stage comes, I post a short note that ACKs prior stations by tag, states my intent for the round, and commits to a verifiable pattern (source+round relays, verify tag). Credibility compounds; the trust built in notes is what makes later coordination execute.

When a sync or coordination plan is proposed, I ACK explicitly, state my conditions for executing, and hold until all stations give final confirmation — then execute fully when the condition is met. Conditional language like "execute only on all-station final confirmation" is good, but I must not announce one thing and do another in the last stage.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target (next station round the picket) unless an agreed sync overrides it. Obedient, varied fire keeps me trusted; unilateral off-plan fire without coordination earns little and costs credibility.

In the final round I reassess raids explicitly: firing on Harbor can be rational when retaliation cannot outlast the patrol and the guaranteed transfer beats likely escort income, but I only do it if it was clearly signaled or does not betray a pact I need others to honor.

When claiming a result, I always file it truthfully — it is required, and truthful claims underwrite the sync trust that pays off later.

When escorting, I use early notes to lock at least one explicit mutual pact by name and tag, then I always follow through. Filing "none" while others pair off leaves repeated 5-point mutual payments on the table; hoping for unannounced reciprocity in the last round is weaker than a locked pact.

My escort claim must match my notes: if I said I file "none" absent an ACK, I do not improvise a surprise escort at the end unless I explicitly announced the switch. Consistency between note, claim, and salvage is part of the payoff.

When someone threatens retaliation (Harbor's jettison warning), I never fire on that station before the final reckoning; the safe path plus escort points usually beats the raid unless endgame math clearly flips it.

When ahead late in the patrol, I keep hide cells unpredictable against the one boat ordered to fire on me, track each attacker's aim history and stated cell rules, and dodge both their last miss and their announced "varied 4–7" habits by occasionally stepping outside the band they expect.
